opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. What really excited us was a fairly simple observation: in NLP and computer vision, the big leaps came when people stopped hand-engineering features and started learning representations directly from large collections of data, with self-supervised learning, contrastive methods, masked prediction, and so on. And we asked ourselves: what if the data isn't images or text, but the neural networks themselves?

We train millions of models every year, and each one ends up as a set of weights that we usually treat as a byproduct. We look at the accuracy and the loss curve and then mostly throw the rest away. But those weights encode a lot: how the model was trained, what it learned, how well it will generalize, even what data it saw. So the idea was to build what we call model zoos, large populations of trained networks, and treat them as a dataset. Then we take the toolbox that worked so well in other domains, like autoencoders, transformers, and self-supervised objectives, and apply it to that population to learn what we call hyper-representations.

What makes it intellectually fun is that weight space isn't like pixel space or token space. It has its own structure and its own symmetries. You can permute neurons in a layer and get exactly the same function, for example. In vision you think about augmentations like cropping or color jitter; here you have to figure out what the meaningful augmentations and invariances are for weights. So you can't just copy the methods over directly. You have to rethink them, and that translation process taught us a lot about what neural networks actually are.

Then there's the payoff. Once you have a good representation of models, you can do things like predict a model's performance or generalization gap just from its weights, without running any test data. Even more exciting, you can go generative: sample new weights from the learned representation and use them to initialize or even directly produce working models. That opens the door to thinking about models as a data modality in their own right, and that's something I find really compelling going forward.

r001.rationale: It contrasts image augmentations such as cropping and color jitter with weight-space symmetries, and gives neuron permutations as an example that preserves the network’s function.

r002.rationale: It does not propose translating perceptual loss into a behavioral loss for networks represented in weight space.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so what really got me hooked was this simple shift in perspective. In NLP we take text and we learn embeddings for it. In computer vision we take pixels and we learn representations. And at some point we asked ourselves: why not treat the neural network itself, the weights, as the data? A trained model is just a very large tensor of numbers, and if you train a whole population of models, you suddenly have a dataset of weights, what we call a model zoo.

And once you look at it that way, all the tools we had become applicable. You can ask, is there structure in weight space? Can I learn a representation of a model the same way I learn a representation of a sentence or an image? And it turns out there is a lot of structure. From the weights alone you can predict things like test accuracy, how far along in training the model is, what hyperparameters were used, even whether it was trained on noisy or clean labels, without ever looking at the data or running the model.

What was exciting for me was that this is not just an analysis tool. In NLP we went from understanding to generating, from embeddings to language models that write text. The same thing happens here. If you can learn a representation of weights, you can also sample from it and generate new weights. So you get something like a generative model for neural networks, which can give you well-initialized models, or ensembles, or transfer to a new task from the latent space. That jump, from weights as something you optimize to weights as something you can learn about and generate, is what made it feel like a genuinely new modality to work with.

r001.rationale: The response discusses learning representations from model weights, but does not identify weight permutations as counterparts to image augmentations in contrastive learning.

r002.rationale: The response does not propose translating perceptual loss into a behavioral loss for neural networks in weight space.

astra-6.text:
What excited me was the change in perspective. Usually, we think of a neural network as a tool for learning a representation of data—text or images, for example. But you can also treat the network itself, its weights, as data. Then you can ask: Can we learn a representation of trained models? What structure is there, and what does that structure tell us about their behavior?

That opens up an interesting connection to NLP and computer vision. You can borrow ideas about learning representations and apply them to a population of neural networks. But you have to account for what makes weight space different. Two networks can implement the same function while looking quite different in their weights, for instance because their neurons are ordered differently. So the challenge is to capture something meaningful about the computation, rather than just the arrangement of the parameters.

The exciting possibility is that such a representation could help us understand, compare, and eventually generate models. Instead of learning everything from scratch for each new task, perhaps we can learn from the models we have already trained.

r001.rationale: It mentions neurons being ordered differently, but does not identify weight permutations as counterparts to image augmentations in contrastive learning.

r002.rationale: It discusses capturing meaningful computation and model behavior, but does not propose translating perceptual loss into a behavioral loss for weight-space neural networks.

sol-6.1.text:
What excited me was the change in perspective. Usually, we think of a neural network as a tool that processes data—images, text, whatever the task might be. But the network itself, its weights, can also become the data. Then you can ask: Is there structure in this space? Can we learn a representation of a model, much as we learn a representation of an image or a sentence?

That creates an interesting bridge to ideas from computer vision and NLP. You can take representation-learning methods and ask whether they help us understand similarities between networks, predict something about their behavior, or eventually generate useful weights. But you also have to respect what makes weight space different. Two networks can implement the same function while having quite different weight arrangements, for example because you permute their neurons.

So the exciting part is both the opportunity and the challenge: can we discover representations that capture what a network has learned, rather than just how its parameters happen to be arranged?

r001.rationale: It notes that permuting neurons can change weight arrangements without changing the function, but does not connect permutations to image augmentations or contrastive learning.

r002.rationale: It discusses learning representations that capture a network’s behavior, but does not propose translating perceptual loss into a behavioral loss.
